newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe calls for unity against National Front.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe calls for unity against National Front.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe urged centre-rightists on Monday to drop out of a municipal election in southern France and unite with Socialists to keep out the far-right National Front (FN).
Juppe, interviewed by France Inter radio about the poll's second round in Vitrolles, said: "What we all want is the list of the (centre-right) candidate which came third to pull out."

The Front's Catherine Megret led the field ahead of outgoing Socialist mayor Jean-Jacques Anglade in the first round, triggering a row among mainstream candidates over how to stop the anti-immigrant FN winning control of its fourth town.
In the fiercely-contested election in Vitrolles near Marseille, Megret ended top with 46.7 percent of the vote.
Anglade trailed on 37.0 percent after a campaign marred by insults and scattered violence. Roger Guichard, candidate of the government's RPR-UDF coalition, had 16.3 percent.
A second round will be held next Sunday because Megret fell short of the 50 percent needed to be elected outright mayor of the depressed, sprawling town of 39,000 people.
Both Anglade and Guichard urged each other to stand down to unite mainstream forces against the Front.

The election is a test of the allure of the National Front ahead of 1998 parliamentary elections and amid record unemployment in France. Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen wants to send home millions of immigrants from third world states.
Jean-Claude Gaudin, mayor of Marseille and an influential UDF leader in the region, also urged Guichard to quit.
But one UDF faction led by Foreign Minister Herve de Charette refused to urge Guichard to stand down, saying: "We should not choose between the plague and cholera."

Megret's husband, Bruno Megret, who is the Front's deputy leader, said Juppe covered himself in shame in supporting Anglade, "a candidate who has been invalidated, stripped of his post, and placed under investigation for forgery".
The Front, which has no seats in parliament, won control of its first three towns in France in nationwide municipal elections in 1995 -- Marignane, Orange and Toulon.

In those elections, Anglade overturned a big Front first round lead to win the Vitrolles municipality on the second round by a wafer-thin 353 votes. The vote was cancelled because of irregularities by Anglade's camp.
Anglade, who said Guichard had no reasonable hope and should stand down, called a rally for Wednesday attended by Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Communist chief Robert Hue.

But Guichard said "two Vitrolles voters out of three have rejected the outgoing mayor. He should pull out if he wants to avoid a Megret victory. But it's up to him to call me." Guichard was due to announce his decision at 1500 GMT.
Megret, beaten by Anglade in 1995, was banned from running this month for exceeding campaign spending limits and was "represented" by his wife, who has scant political experience.
Bruno Megret says he will be her chief adviser if she wins, and that Front policies of priority for white French people will help bring down unemployment of 19 percent in the town.
